extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in analytic number theory
extracted.subtask_description: Encyclopedic overview of the Mertens conjecture: definition of the Mertens function, the conjecture statement, history, disproof, computational results, bounds on counterexamples, and connections to the Riemann hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Mertens function and conjecture statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Mertens function M(n) = sum_{1 <= k <= n} mu(k) where mu(k) is the Möbius function; the Mertens conjecture is that for all n > 1, |M(n)| < sqrt(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently define m(n) := M(n)/sqrt(n); the conjecture asserts -1 < m(n) < 1. Attribution: conjectured by Stieltjes (1885) and by Franz Mertens (1897).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof by Odlyzko and te Riele (1985)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mertens conjecture was disproved in 1985 by Andrew Odlyzko and Herman te Riele.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They used the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL) lattice basis reduction algorithm to show quantitatively that the conjecture is false, proving liminf m(n) < -1.009 and limsup m(n) > 1.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative bounds on liminf and limsup of m(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Results giving explicit bounds for the oscillation limits of m(n): e.g. liminf m(n) < -1.009 and limsup m(n) > 1.06 (Odlyzko & te Riele), later improvements such as liminf m(n) < -1.837625 and limsup m(n) > 1.826054 (Hurst, 2016).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These bounds demonstrate that m(n) does exceed the conjectured [-1,1] interval infinitely often; methods and improvements are computational and analytic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounds on where the first counterexample may occur
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper and lower bounds on the size of the smallest n violating |M(n)| < sqrt(n): initially shown to lie below e^{3.21×10^{64}} and above 10^{16}; later upper bounds were successively lowered to e^{1.59×10^{40}}, e^{1.017×10^{29}}, and (2024) e^{1.96×10^{19}}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No explicit counterexample is known; the bounds give astronomically large ranges for the possible first counterexample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to the Riemann hypothesis (equivalence of growth bounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: M(x) = O(x^{1/2+epsilon}) for every epsilon > 0 is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis; the (stronger) Mertens hypothesis M(x) = O(x^{1/2}) would have implied the Riemann hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The equivalence is derived from representing 1/ζ(s) as a Dirichlet series and as a Mellin transform of M(x); analytic continuation and growth conditions of M(x) correspond to properties of ζ(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral / Mellin-transform representation linking M and 1/ζ
rubrics_metrics.description: 1/ζ(s) = ∫_0^∞ x^{-s} dM(x) and, after integration by parts, (1/(s ζ(s))) = ∫_0^∞ x^{-s} M(x) (dx/x); inversion gives M(x) = (1/(2π i)) ∫_{σ - i∞}^{σ + i∞} x^s /(s ζ(s)) ds (valid for 1 < σ < 2, and for 1/2 < σ < 2 assuming RH).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formulas explain how analytic properties of ζ(s) control the growth of M(x) and are the technical backbone of the RH–Mertens connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/computational data and extreme known values
rubrics_metrics.description: Computed maximal known values of m(n): Cohen & Dress (1979) found m(n) ≈ 0.570591 at n = 7,766,842,813; Kuznetsov (2011) found m(n) ≈ -0.585768 at a very large n; Hurst (2016) computed M(n) for every n ≤ 10^16 without finding larger m(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computations provide concrete data points but do not contradict asymptotic results showing eventual violations of the conjecture; Kotnik & te Riele (2006) showed infinitely many n with m(n) > 1.2184 without giving explicit n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic and probabilistic expectations for growth of m(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristics: replacing μ by a random ±1 sequence gives partial sums of order sqrt(n log log n) (law of the iterated logarithm), suggesting m(n) might grow like sqrt(log log n); other conjectures (Gonek) propose growth like (log log log n)^{5/4}, supported by heuristic arguments under RH and assumptions on zero distribution (Ng, 2004).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are heuristic/speculative expectations on the typical size of m(n), not proven theorems; different heuristics give different slow-growing orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological note: use of lattice reduction (LLL) in analytic number theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The disproof employed the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász lattice basis reduction algorithm to produce the contradictory bounds showing the conjecture false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highlights a computational/algorithmic technique applied to derive analytic-number-theoretic consequences; the Wikipedia article cites this as central to Odlyzko & te Riele's work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical provenance and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The conjecture was conjectured by Stieltjes in an 1885 letter and again in print by Franz Mertens (1897); its disproof is a striking example of a conjecture with strong computational support being false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames the Mertens conjecture historically and pedagogically, emphasizing its role in illustrating pitfalls of inferring universality from finite computation.
